summary.en: Tim Berners-Lee submits his proposal for the World Wide Web at CERN in March 1989. By the end of 1990 the system is working.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of editorial magazine illustration from the 1980s–90s, not a historical image.

summary.en: On 24 February 2022 Russia attacked Ukraine, a major escalation of the war between the two countries that began in 2014. It is the largest and deadliest war in Europe since the Second World War, and it is still going on.

intro.en: Ukraine became independent when the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991, and in 1994 Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom promised in the Budapest Memorandum to respect its borders. After the protests in Kyiv, President Viktor Yanukovych fled to Russia in February 2014. That same month Russian soldiers without rank insignia began occupying Crimea, and in March 2014 Russia annexed the peninsula after a referendum held under occupation. In April 2014 the war in Donbas began, where armed Russian paramilitary groups seized towns and proclaimed people's republics in Donetsk and Luhansk. Russia secretly supported the separatists with soldiers and weapons, and by the end of 2021 14,200–14,400 people had died. In the autumn of 2021 Russia massed troops at the borders but denied that an attack was planned. On 24 February 2022 President Vladimir Putin announced a “special military operation”, and Russia attacked Ukraine from Belarus, from Russia and from Crimea. On 2 March 2022 the UN General Assembly deplored in the strongest terms Russia's aggression against Ukraine and demanded that Russia immediately withdraw all its forces (resolution ES-11/1).

members.en: Ukraine, with weapons, training, money and intelligence from, among others, the United States and European countries. The aid is coordinated in a group of over fifty countries, including all NATO members.

Russia, with forces from the self-proclaimed people's republics of Donetsk and Luhansk. Belarus allowed Russia to attack and fire missiles from its territory. North Korea has supplied missiles and sent soldiers to Kursk Oblast in 2024. According to the United States and Ukraine, Iran has supplied drones, which Iran denies.

outcome.en: The war is ongoing. Russian troops occupy about a fifth of Ukraine. In September 2022 Russia declared four partly occupied Ukrainian provinces annexed, which Ukraine, the United States, the EU and the UN condemned as illegal. During 2025 Russia advanced slowly in eastern Ukraine and, according to reports, took the city of Pokrovsk in early 2026. During 2026 Ukraine has regained ground in several counterattacks, and Russia's spring offensive was judged by military analysts to have failed. The peace negotiations have stalled, and Russia has rejected demands for a ceasefire. Of Ukraine's 41 million inhabitants, about 8 million have fled within the country and 6–7 million to other countries.

casualties.en: Civilians: the UN human rights office (OHCHR) had by 31 August 2026 recorded 17,257 civilians killed and 53,693 injured in Ukraine since 24 February 2022, and assesses that the real figures are higher. Soldiers: losses are state secrets in both countries, and the parties exaggerate their opponent's losses, so the figures are uncertain and differ widely. By 20 October 2026 the BBC and Mediazona had identified 282,993 dead Russian soldiers by name, and the BBC estimated that 512,000–626,000 Russian soldiers (excluding the separatists' forces) had died by mid-October 2026. By 25 October 2026 the UALosses project had identified 106,285 dead and 105,786 missing Ukrainian soldiers. The UCDP research programme at Uppsala University counts about 373,000 battle-related deaths in 2022–2025 (range 312,000–575,000), soldiers and civilians killed in fighting between Russia and Ukraine. In total, 1.27–2 million soldiers and civilians are estimated to have been killed or wounded up to June 2026.

summary.en: Russian forces try to take the capital Kyiv from the north, including from Belarus, but meet fierce resistance. After Ukrainian counterattacks, Russia begins to withdraw on 29 March, and by 2 April 2022 Kyiv and Kyiv Oblast are again under Ukrainian control.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 24 February–2 April 2022 and Wikidata 25 February–31 March 2022. The year and the place agree.

caption.en: Women, children and elderly people make their way across the Irpin River after the bridge to Kyiv has been blown up, 8 March 2022. Photograph by Yan Boechat for Voice of America. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 2 March 2022 the UN General Assembly, at an emergency special session, deplores in the strongest terms Russia's aggression against Ukraine and demands that Russia immediately and unconditionally withdraw all its forces. Resolution ES-11/1, “Aggression against Ukraine”, is adopted with 141 votes in favour, 5 against and 35 abstentions. It also deplores Belarus's involvement. A draft in the Security Council had been blocked by a veto the day after the invasion.

text.en: Wikidata's entry on the resolution has no date or place, so they could not be compared with a second, independent source. The date and the vote counts were checked in the UN Digital Library, the place according to Wikipedia.

summary.en: Russian troops take the town of Bucha on 27 February 2022. After they have withdrawn, images and film emerge on 1 April showing that civilians were killed during the occupation. The UN human rights chief has documented unlawful killings of at least 73 civilians, and according to local authorities 458 dead were found. Russia denies responsibility, but its claims have been refuted by several investigators.

Russian forces besiege the port city of Mariupol from the start of the war, and the city is largely destroyed. The last Ukrainian soldiers in the Azovstal steelworks surrender on 20 May 2022. The UN has confirmed that 1,348 civilians were killed in the city, but assesses that the real number is thousands higher.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the siege began on 24 February 2022 and Wikidata on 25 February. The end, 20 May 2022, and the place agree.

summary.en: On 6 September 2022 Ukraine launches a surprise counteroffensive in Kharkiv Oblast, near Balakliia. Within a few days the towns of Izium and Kupiansk are retaken, and by early October Ukraine has recaptured over 500 settlements and about 12,000 square kilometres.

After Ukraine's counteroffensive in the south, the Russian forces withdraw across the Dnipro River on 9–11 November 2022. On 11 November Ukrainian soldiers enter Kherson, the first major city that Russia took after the invasion.

text.en: Wikidata's entry gives only the year and no place, so the day and the place could not be compared with a second, independent source. The information comes from Wikipedia.

summary.en: Russian forces, mainly the Wagner Group with recruited prisoners, attack the town of Bakhmut in Donetsk Oblast from the summer of 2022. Some military analysts count the battle as the bloodiest since the Second World War. On 20 May 2023 Wagner claims that the whole town has been taken.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the battle began in July 2022 (the start date is unclear) and ended on 20 May 2023 (there is no consensus on the end). Wikidata gives 9 August 2022–7 January 2024. The place agrees.

summary.en: In early June 2023 Ukraine launches an offensive in Zaporizhzhia and Donetsk Oblast to break through the Russian lines, which have extensive fortifications and minefields. Ukraine retakes 14 villages, including Robotyne, but by December 2023 the offensive is widely judged to have stalled without reaching its goals.

On 6 August 2024 Ukrainian forces enter Russia's Kursk Oblast, the largest cross-border attack since the invasion. They take, among other places, the town of Sudzha. From November 2024 North Korean soldiers fight on the Russian side, and by March 2025 Russia has pushed back most of the Ukrainian forces.

The war began when Iraq invaded Iran in September 1980 and ended with a ceasefire negotiated by the UN in August 1988. It was marked by trench warfare and deliberate attacks on civilians, including Iraqi attacks with chemical weapons. Around 450,000–500,000 people died, and the border remained the same as before the war.

title.en: About the start of the war

text.en: The war is counted here from Iraq's invasion of Iran on 22 September 1980. Iraq claims that the war began as early as 4 September 1980, when Iran shelled Iraqi towns.

intro.en: After the Islamic Revolution of 1979, Iran was led by Ruhollah Khomeini. According to the sources, the Iraqi government under President Saddam Hussein above all wanted to prevent Iran from exporting its new state ideology to Iraq, and feared that Shia Muslim Iran would make Iraq's Shia Muslim majority rise up against the Sunni-dominated Ba'athist regime. Iraq also wanted to replace Iran as the leading power in the Persian Gulf. The countries had long disagreed about the border, and Iraq wanted to take back the eastern bank of the Shatt al-Arab, which it had ceded to Iran in the Algiers Agreement of 1975. Iraq expected a quick victory, since Iran was weakened after the revolution.

members.en: Iraq, with support from, among others, the United States, the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union, France, Italy, Yugoslavia, most Arab countries and the National Council of Resistance of Iran (NCRI).
Iran, with support from, among others, the Kurdish parties KDP and PUK, Syria, Libya, North Korea, China, South Yemen, Pakistan, Cuba and Israel.

outcome.en: The outcome was a draw, and both countries have claimed to have won. Iraq's invasion had stalled by December 1980, and by June 1982 Iran had retaken all of its territory and then entered Iraq. During five years of Iranian offensives and Iraqi counteroffensives the situation became deadlocked. After heavy losses Iran accepted a ceasefire under UN Security Council Resolution 598, which took effect in August 1988. The war did not lead to any lasting border changes, and neither country received war reparations. Iraq kept certain Iranian border areas until August 1990.

casualties.en: Around 450,000–500,000 dead according to the estimates reported by Wikipedia (Pfetsch and Rohloff 2013, Encyclopaedia Britannica). Estimates for soldiers differ widely: 200,000–600,000 dead on Iran's side and 105,000–500,000 on Iraq's. More than 100,000 civilians died. In addition, 50,000–200,000 Kurdish civilians were killed in Iraq's Anfal campaign, which is not included in the figures. The figures are estimates and are given as ranges.

summary.en: On 22 September 1980 Iraqi aircraft bomb ten Iranian air bases, and the next day Iraqi troops cross the border in three simultaneous attacks. Four of six divisions are sent against oil-rich Khuzestan. The port city of Khorramshahr is taken on 26 October. Iran puts up fierce resistance, and the invasion stalls in early December 1980.

On 24 April 1982 Iran launches an offensive to retake the occupied parts of Khuzestan. After two days of hard fighting, Iranian forces retake Khorramshahr on 24 May 1982. It is seen as a turning point in the war, and the day is celebrated every year in Iran.

caption.en: Iranian soldiers celebrate at the Jameh Mosque in Khorramshahr after the city has been retaken, 24 May 1982. Photograph by Amir Ali Javadian. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Iraq has been driven out of almost all of Iran, and Khomeini rejects Iraq's peace offers. On 13 July 1982 Iran attacks near Basra in Iraq, with three assaults and large waves of infantry. It is counted as one of the largest land battles since the Second World War. Iraq holds its ground, and the war becomes a deadlocked war of position.

text.en: Wikipedia states both that the offensive lasted from 13 July to 3 August 1982 and that it lasted six weeks. Wikidata gives only 3 August 1982 and no place, so the place could not be compared with a second source.

summary.en: From May 1981 Iraq attacks merchant ships to and from Iranian ports in the Persian Gulf. From 1984 Iraq also strikes the oil port on Kharg Island, Iran's most important export port, and Iran responds with attacks of its own. Up to 1988 Iraq carries out 283 and Iran 168 attacks on merchant ships.

text.en: Wikipedia counts the Tanker War from 1981, when Iraq began attacking merchant ships. Wikidata instead gives 1 February 1984 as the start. The end, 4 August 1988, agrees in both.

summary.en: In February 1986 Iranian forces cross the Shatt al-Arab and take the al-Faw Peninsula, which connects Iraq to the Persian Gulf. Iraq is thereby shut off from the sea. Iran holds the peninsula for a month against Iraqi counterattacks, including with chemical weapons, until the situation becomes deadlocked. Iraq retook the peninsula towards the end of the war.

text.en: Wikipedia dates the battle to 10 February–10 March 1986 but also says that the Iranian operation began on 9 February. Wikidata gives 11 February 1986. The year and the place agree.

summary.en: On 16 March 1988, two days after Iran has taken the town, Iraq attacks Halabja with chemical weapons. Between 3,200 and 5,000 people, most of them Kurdish civilians, are killed and 7,000–10,000 injured. The UN investigation found that mustard gas and nerve agents had been used. The attack was part of Iraq's Anfal campaign and is the largest attack with chemical weapons against a populated area in history. The US military intelligence service first pointed to Iran, but most of the evidence later showed that Iraq was behind it.

On 20 July 1987 the UN Security Council unanimously demands in Resolution 598 that Iran and Iraq immediately stop fighting and withdraw to the border. Iraq accepts quickly, but Iran only almost a year later. The resolution takes effect on 8 August 1988, and the ceasefire comes into force at three in the morning on 20 August. UN observers monitor the border until 1991.

text.en: Wikidata's entry on Resolution 598 has no date, so the dates could not be compared with a second, independent source. The information comes from Wikipedia.

summary.en: A civil war in 1988–1998 on the island of Bougainville in Papua New Guinea, which began with protests against the large copper mine at Panguna and became a war for independence. Bougainville's President John Momis has called it the largest conflict in Oceania since the Second World War. The peace led to autonomy and a referendum on independence.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 1988–1998 and mentions the Lincoln Agreement in January 1998 as the road to peace. Wikidata gives more precisely 1 December 1988 to 20 April 1998; that end date is not in Wikipedia's article.

intro.en: The Panguna mine on Bougainville opened in 1972 and was then the world's largest open-pit mine. It provided more than 45 per cent of Papua New Guinea's export earnings, but the people of Bougainville received only a small share of the profit, the mine's waste poisoned the Jaba River and thousands of workers came from other parts of the country. Bougainville had already tried to break away in 1975. In 1988 the landowner Francis Ona and his Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRA) began to sabotage the mine, and when the government sent police and the military it became an uprising for independence. The war also became a civil war between clans and militias on the island.

members.en: The Bougainville Revolutionary Army (BRA) under Francis Ona and the military commander Sam Kauona, and the Bougainville Interim Government (BIG) with Ona as president and Joseph Kabui as vice-president. The BRA was dominated by the Nasioi clan, and several armed gangs claimed to belong to the BRA without obeying its leadership.

The Papua New Guinea Defence Force (PNGDF) and the police's riot squads, with weapons, helicopters, patrol boats and training from Australia, as well as local militias on Bougainville, “the resistance” (Bougainville Resistance Forces), which were armed by the army. In 1997 the government tried to hire mercenaries from Sandline International.

outcome.en: After the Sandline affair and the change of government in 1997, talks in New Zealand led to a ceasefire and the Lincoln Agreement in January 1998. Unarmed peace monitors from, among others, New Zealand, Australia, Fiji and Vanuatu came to the island. A peace agreement in 2001 gave Bougainville autonomy, and in 2005 the first autonomous government was elected. In a non-binding referendum in 2019 an overwhelming majority voted for independence, and under an agreement in 2021 Bougainville is to become independent in September 2027 if Papua New Guinea's government approves. The Panguna mine has been closed since 1989.

casualties.en: Estimates differ widely. The Australian government assessed that 15,000–20,000 people may have died, other sources give about 10,000 dead from violence or disease, and more cautious assessments count 1,000–2,000 dead in fighting. More than 300 of Papua New Guinea's soldiers died. In the mid-1990s over 60,000 people from Bougainville lived in refugee camps, and thousands fled to the Solomon Islands.

summary.en: Francis Ona, a landowner from Panguna and a former employee of the mine, forms the Bougainville Revolutionary Army in 1988 and begins to sabotage the mine. The resistance concerns the environmental destruction and the fact that the profit goes to Papua New Guinea instead of to Bougainville. The government sends the police riot squads and the military, and the fighting spreads across the island.
On 15 May 1989 Panguna, one of the world's largest copper and gold mines, is closed. The mining company's last staff leave the island in March 1990, and the mine has not reopened.

text.en: The date is based only on Wikipedia. The place is the mine according to Wikidata.

summary.en: In early 1990 Papua New Guinea withdraws its forces and leaves Bougainville to the BRA. In May 1990 Francis Ona unilaterally declares independence and forms an interim government with himself as president. The government responds with a blockade of the island that lasts until the ceasefire in 1994, and in some places until 1997.

text.en: Wikipedia's article on the conflict gives May 1990. The article on Francis Ona says in one place that independence was declared in 1989 and in another that it happened in response to the blockade in 1990.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of a documentary newspaper illustration from the 1970s, not a historical image.

summary.en: Under Prime Minister Paias Wingti the government's policy hardens. In February 1993 the army, together with local militias, retakes the provincial capital Arawa. The town is largely destroyed during the war, and the capital is moved to Buka.

text.en: The date is based only on Wikipedia. The place is Arawa according to both Wikipedia and Wikidata.

summary.en: Prime Minister Julius Chan has secretly hired mercenaries from the British company Sandline International to retake Panguna. When this becomes known, army chief Jerry Singirok refuses to let them operate, and in March 1997 the country is close to a military coup, with large protests outside parliament. The contract is cancelled, the mercenaries leave the country and Chan resigns on 26 March. Bill Skate, who becomes prime minister in July, seeks peace instead.

Under the new Prime Minister Bill Skate, talks in Honiara and in Burnham in New Zealand in 1997 lead to a ceasefire and an unarmed monitoring group led by New Zealand. Continued talks in Christchurch with the BRA leaders Sam Kauona and Joseph Kabui, but without Francis Ona, lead to the Lincoln Agreement in January 1998. Papua New Guinea begins to withdraw its soldiers, and a peace agreement follows in 2001.

text.en: The information is based only on Wikipedia, which gives the year 1997 for the ceasefire and January 1998 for the Lincoln Agreement without exact dates. The point on the map is the Burnham military camp.

summary.en: A war between Iraq and a coalition of 42 countries led by the United States, after Iraq had invaded its neighbour Kuwait on 2 August 1990. The coalition bombed Iraq and Kuwait from January 1991 and drove the Iraqi troops out of Kuwait with a ground offensive at the end of February.

intro.en: After the war against Iran (1980–1988), Iraq was heavily in debt, above all to Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, which refused to write off the debts. Iraq accused Kuwait of pumping more oil than OPEC's quotas allowed, which pushed down the oil price, and of drilling at a slant under the border into the Iraqi oil field of Rumaila. According to oil workers in the area, the last claim was fabricated. Iraq also laid claim to Kuwaiti territory. At talks in Jeddah, Iraq demanded 10 billion dollars for lost oil revenue, and Kuwait offered 500 million. Iraq responded by invading Kuwait on 2 August 1990. Within hours the UN Security Council demanded that Iraq withdraw and imposed a total trade embargo. On 29 November 1990 the Council gave Iraq until 15 January 1991 to leave Kuwait. After that, member states were allowed to use “all necessary means”.

members.en: 42 countries led by the United States. The largest contributions came from the United States, Saudi Arabia, the United Kingdom and Egypt. Other participants included France, Kuwait, Syria, Canada and Italy, and Sweden too appears in the source's list. Commanders included President George H. W. Bush and General Norman Schwarzkopf.
Saddam Hussein's government and the Iraqi army, with the elite Republican Guard. According to the source's estimate, Iraq had over a million soldiers, of whom about 600,000 were in Kuwait.

outcome.en: The coalition halted the ground offensive after a hundred hours and declared a ceasefire on 28 February 1991. Kuwait became independent again, and the emir returned on 15 March. Saddam Hussein remained in power. During the retreat the Iraqi troops set fire to hundreds of oil wells in Kuwait (the source gives, in different places, over 600, almost 700 and 737). Immediately after the war the government crushed uprisings in southern and northern Iraq, where an estimated 25,000–100,000 people were killed, and the coalition imposed no-fly zones over northern and southern Iraq. UN sanctions and weapons inspections continued, and in 2003 a new US-led coalition invaded Iraq.

casualties.en: Estimates differ widely, especially for Iraq. The coalition lost 292 dead, of whom 147 in combat, and Kuwait about 420 soldiers and over 1,000 civilians. Estimates of dead Iraqi soldiers range from 20,000–26,000 (Project on Defense Alternatives) to at least 65,000 (Les Aspin, chairman of the US House Armed Services Committee); the source's compilation gives 20,000–50,000. About 3,700 Iraqi civilians were killed directly according to the Project on Defense Alternatives and about 13,000 according to a study by Beth Osborne Daponte. The organisation Medact estimated in 2022 all Iraqi deaths from the war, direct and indirect and including the uprisings afterwards, at 142,500–206,000. The UCDP research programme at Uppsala University counts 22,805–27,261 battle-related deaths in the conflict in 1990–1991 (best estimate 22,848). UCDP counts only deaths in fighting between organised parties, including civilians killed in the fighting, but not deliberate violence against civilians or indirect deaths from disease and starvation.

summary.en: At midnight on 2 August 1990 Iraqi troops cross the border and attack Kuwait City by land, air and sea. Within twelve hours most resistance has ceased, and the emir and the government flee to Saudi Arabia. On 4 August Iraq controls the country, and on 28 August Iraq declares Kuwait annexed.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 2–4 August 1990. Wikidata has the same end date, 4 August 1990, but gives the start year as 2009, which looks like a typing error in Wikidata.

summary.en: On the night of 17 January 1991, two days after the UN deadline, Operation Desert Storm begins with air strikes against targets in Iraq and in occupied Kuwait, many of them in Baghdad. Over five weeks the coalition flies over 100,000 sorties. Iraq fires missiles at Israel and Saudi Arabia, but fails to split the coalition.

text.en: The article on the air war and Wikidata give 17 January 1991 as the start, with the first attack at 02.38 Baghdad time. Wikipedia's article on the Gulf War says 16 January in one place. The year and the place agree.

summary.en: On 29 January 1991 Iraqi armoured units from Kuwait enter Saudi Arabia and take the lightly defended town of Khafji. Saudi Arabian and Qatari troops retake the town by 1 February, supported by US aircraft and artillery. It was the war's first major ground battle.

At four in the morning on 24 February 1991 the coalition's ground troops enter Kuwait, and at the same time other units attack into southern Iraq. Most Iraqi soldiers surrender after brief fighting, but at Kuwait International Airport one unit fights for several hours. On 27 February Saddam Hussein orders a retreat, and the retreating troops set fire to hundreds of oil wells. Kuwait is declared liberated.

text.en: The articles on the Gulf War and on the liberation of Kuwait state, like Wikidata, that the ground offensive began on 24 February 1991. Wikipedia's article on the invasion of Kuwait says 23 February, and according to the article on the Gulf War there was already fighting that day.

caption.en: Abandoned Iraqi tanks along the road between Basra and Kuwait near Kuwait City, 26 February 1991. Photograph by PHC Holmes, US Navy. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 26 February 1991 American and British armoured units of VII Corps meet the Republican Guard's Tawakalna Division in the desert. The battle has been named after a coordinate line on the maps used to measure the advance. It ends in a coalition victory and is counted among the largest armoured battles in US history.

text.en: Wikipedia's and Wikidata's coordinates for the battle lie about 35 kilometres apart, both in the desert in south-eastern Iraq. Wikipedia's are shown here.

summary.en: On 28 February 1991, a hundred hours after the ground offensive began, the coalition halts its advance and declares a ceasefire. A ceasefire agreement is then negotiated at a conference on Iraqi territory occupied by the coalition. The day after the ceasefire, an uprising breaks out in Basra.

text.en: The ceasefire has no entry of its own in Wikidata, so the event could not be compared with a second source. Wikidata gives the same end date for the whole war, 28 February 1991.

summary.en: A war in Afghanistan that began when a US-led coalition invaded the country after the terrorist attacks of 11 September 2001 and overthrew the Taliban government. The Taliban then waged a guerrilla war against the new government and the foreign troops, and in 2021 they took power again.

intro.en: On 11 September 2001, 19 members of al-Qaeda hijacked four passenger aircraft in the United States. Two were flown into the World Trade Center in New York, one into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, and the fourth crashed in a field in Pennsylvania. 2,996 people died, the hijackers included. Al-Qaeda's leader Osama bin Laden, who had planned the attacks, was in Afghanistan, where the Taliban had taken Kabul in 1996 and in 2001 ruled most of the country. US President George W. Bush demanded that the Taliban hand over bin Laden and close al-Qaeda's camps. The Taliban refused and demanded proof of his guilt, and later offered to hand him over to a third country if the bombing stopped. The United States rejected the offers, and on 7 October 2001 the invasion began. Scholars disagree about whether the invasion was lawful under international law: the United States and its allies cited the right of self-defence in the UN Charter.

name.en: The United States, its allies and the Afghan government

members.en: At the invasion the United States and the United Kingdom together with, among others, France, Canada, Italy, Germany, Australia and New Zealand, and the Afghan Northern Alliance. From December 2001 the UN-authorised force ISAF with troops from many countries, among them Sweden. ISAF was at its largest in 2011, with about 140,000 foreign soldiers. On the Afghan side, from 2004, stood the Islamic Republic of Afghanistan, with Presidents Hamid Karzai and Ashraf Ghani.

The Taliban's Islamic Emirate of Afghanistan under Mullah Omar, al-Qaeda, the Haqqani network and other Islamist groups. From 2015 the Islamic State was also active in Afghanistan, but that group sometimes also fought against the Taliban.

outcome.en: On 29 February 2020 the United States and the Taliban concluded an agreement in Doha, Qatar, that the American troops would leave Afghanistan. The Afghan government was not a party to the agreement. While the troops were being withdrawn, the Taliban launched a final offensive on 1 May 2021, and on 15 August they entered Kabul without resistance. President Ghani fled, and the Taliban declared the war over and reinstated the Islamic Emirate. On 30 August the last American military aircraft left the country. The war became the longest in US history. When Kabul fell, 2.6 million Afghans were still refugees and a further 4 million internally displaced.

casualties.en: Estimates differ. According to the Costs of War Project, about 176,000 people were killed, of whom 46,319 Afghan civilians. The UCDP research programme at Uppsala University counts 224,794–286,751 battle-related deaths in Afghanistan in the calendar years 2001–2021 (best estimate 238,796). UCDP counts only deaths in fighting between organised parties, including civilians killed in the fighting, but not deliberate violence against civilians or indirect deaths from disease and starvation. Medical organisations, among them IPPNW, estimated the number of civilians killed at 106,000–170,000. Among the dead were 66,000–92,000 from the Afghan security forces, 52,893–80,000 or more Taliban and 3,579 coalition soldiers, of whom 2,330 Americans. In the neighbouring insurgency in north-western Pakistan a further 66,650 people were killed.

summary.en: On 7 October 2001 the United States and the United Kingdom launch air strikes against 31 targets in Afghanistan, under the name Operation Enduring Freedom. American special forces and the CIA support the Northern Alliance, which takes one city after another from the Taliban. Kabul is taken on 13 November, and by 17 December the Taliban government has been overthrown. Most of the Taliban and al-Qaeda leaders escape to Pakistan or to remote mountain areas.

caption.en: American special forces with soldiers of the Northern Alliance west of Kunduz in November 2001. Photograph from the US Army. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 30 November 2001 American, British and German units, together with Afghan militias, attack the Tora Bora cave complex, where the CIA had tracked Osama bin Laden. The complex is destroyed, but bin Laden escapes, probably around 15 December, and crosses the border into Pakistan.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 30 November–17 December 2001. Wikidata gives 6–17 December 2001. The year and the place agree.

summary.en: On 2–18 March 2002 about 1,700 American soldiers, flown in by helicopter, and 1,000 pro-government Afghan militiamen fight 300–1,000 al-Qaeda and Taliban fighters in the Shah-i-Kot Valley. It was the first major battle since Tora Bora and the first in which many American soldiers took part directly in combat in Afghanistan.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 2–18 March 2002. Wikidata gives 1–18 March 2002. The year and the place agree.

summary.en: On 13 February 2010 about 15,000 Afghan, American, British, Canadian, Danish and Estonian soldiers begin an offensive against Marjah in Helmand, which had long been controlled by the Taliban and drug traffickers. It was the war's largest joint operation so far. The NATO forces took Marjah, but when they later withdrew, the Taliban took the town again.

After an offensive that began on 1 May 2021, at the same time as the foreign troops were being withdrawn, the Taliban reach Kabul on 15 August and enter the city without resistance. President Ashraf Ghani flees, the Islamic Republic falls and the Taliban declare the war over.

Between 14 and 30 August 2021 the United States and its allies fly out more than 123,000 people from the airport in Kabul: diplomats, foreign nationals and Afghans who had worked with the coalition or were at risk of persecution. On 30 August the last American military aircraft leaves the country, and the American military presence in Afghanistan is over.

text.en: The event has no entry of its own in Wikidata, so it could not be compared with a second source. Wikidata gives the same end date for the whole war, 30 August 2021.

summary.en: A war in Iraq that began when a US-led coalition invaded the country in March 2003 and overthrew Saddam Hussein's government. The invasion was followed by a long insurgency against the foreign troops and the new Iraqi government, and a civil war between Shia and Sunni Muslims. The last American troops left Iraq in December 2011.

title.en: About the end of the war

text.en: Wikipedia states that the war ended on 18 December 2011, when the last American combat troops left Iraq. Wikidata gives 15 December 2011, when a ceremony in Baghdad formally ended the American mission.

intro.en: After the Gulf War the UN demanded that Iraq get rid of all weapons of mass destruction. Iraq obstructed the weapons inspections and stopped them completely in 1998, the same year that the United States made regime change in Iraq official policy. After the terrorist attacks of 11 September 2001, Iraq became part of the US war on terror, and in October 2002 the American Congress authorised President George W. Bush to use military force against Iraq. The main reasons given were that Iraq had weapons of mass destruction and supported al-Qaeda. Both claims proved to be false: no stockpiles of weapons of mass destruction were found, and the 9/11 Commission found in 2004 no credible evidence of a link between Saddam Hussein and al-Qaeda. UN Secretary-General Kofi Annan called the invasion illegal under the UN Charter, while the United States cited the right of self-defence and earlier Security Council decisions. On 20 March 2003 the invasion began, without a declaration of war.

name.en: US-led coalition and Iraq's new government

members.en: At the invasion the “coalition of the willing” with the United States, the United Kingdom, Australia and Poland, together with Kurdish peshmerga and the Iraqi opposition. During the insurgency Iraq's new government and security forces, the Multi-National Force in Iraq and the Sunni so-called Awakening Councils.

name.en: Saddam Hussein's government and the insurgent groups

members.en: At the invasion Saddam Hussein's Ba'athist government and the Iraqi army. Afterwards a large number of insurgent groups: Sunni Muslim groups such as al-Qaeda in Iraq, later the Islamic State of Iraq, and Ba'athist groups, as well as Shia Muslim militias such as the Mahdi Army.

outcome.en: Saddam Hussein was captured in December 2003 and executed in 2006. Iraq held multi-party elections in 2005. From 2006 there was a civil war between Shia and Sunni Muslims, and in 2007 the United States sent more troops, which according to the source helped to stabilise parts of the country. In 2008 the United States and Iraq agreed that the American forces would leave the country before the end of 2011, and on 18 December 2011 the last combat troops left Iraq. In 2007 about 2.3 million Iraqis were internally displaced and about 2 million had fled to neighbouring countries. The war contributed to the rise of the Islamic State, which in 2014 took Mosul and Tikrit, and the United States then returned with air strikes. A British inquiry, the Chilcot Report (2016), concluded that the war was not necessary because peaceful alternatives had not been fully tried.

casualties.en: Estimates differ widely. The organisation Iraq Body Count counted 103,160–113,728 documented civilian deaths from violence up to December 2011. Statistical surveys, which also count combatants and indirect deaths, arrive at considerably higher figures: about 151,000 up to July 2006 (Iraq Family Health Survey), about 655,000 up to July 2006 (the journal The Lancet), about 405,000 up to June 2011 (the journal PLOS Medicine) and over a million up to August 2007 (the polling institute Opinion Research Business). The coalition lost 4,826 soldiers, of whom 4,508 Americans and 179 British, and Iraq's new security forces 17,690. The UCDP research programme at Uppsala University counts 24,337–35,719 battle-related deaths in the calendar years 2003–2011 (best estimate 25,765), of which 7,927–13,814 during the invasion in 2003. UCDP counts only deaths in fighting between organised parties, including civilians killed in the fighting, but not deliberate violence against civilians or indirect deaths from disease and starvation.

summary.en: At 05.34 Baghdad time on 20 March 2003 the invasion of Iraq begins, without a declaration of war. About 250,000 American, 45,000 British, 2,000 Australian and almost 200 Polish soldiers have gathered in Kuwait, and in the north Kurdish peshmerga fight. Baghdad falls on 9 April and Tikrit on 15 April. On 1 May President Bush gives his “Mission Accomplished” speech.

caption.en: American Marines lead Iraqi prisoners of war to a collection area in the desert on 21 March 2003. Photograph by Brian L. Wickliffe, USMC. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: Three weeks into the invasion, on 3 April 2003, American troops reach Baghdad. Over 2,000 Iraqi soldiers and 34 coalition soldiers are killed in the fighting. On 9 April the city falls, and Saddam Hussein's 24 years in power are over. The overthrow is followed by looting of public buildings and increased crime.

text.en: Wikipedia gives 3–9 April 2003. Wikidata gives 3–12 April 2003. The year and the place agree.

summary.en: On 13 December 2003 American special forces and soldiers of the 4th Infantry Division find Saddam Hussein hiding in a hole in the ground at a farm outside ad-Dawr. He offers no resistance. The operation, called Red Dawn, was preceded by months of searching. Saddam Hussein was executed in 2006.

On 7 November 2004 American, Iraqi and British forces attack the insurgent groups in Fallujah, among them al-Qaeda in Iraq. For six weeks the war's bloodiest fighting takes place, which has been described as the hardest street fighting for American troops since the Vietnam War. Just over 100 coalition soldiers are killed, as are 1,200–2,000 insurgents according to the coalition's estimate. 581–670 civilians were killed according to Iraq Body Count and about 800 according to the Red Cross.

On 22 February 2006 the golden dome of the al-Askari Mosque in Samarra, one of the holiest sites of Shia Islam, is destroyed by two bombs. No one is killed in the attack itself, and no one claimed responsibility. President Bush pointed to al-Qaeda in Iraq, which denied involvement. Revenge attacks with over 1,000 dead within a few days followed, and the bombing triggered the civil war between Shia and Sunni Muslims, which lasted until 2008.

On 15 December 2011 the American mission in Iraq formally ends at a ceremony in Baghdad. The last 500 soldiers leave the country on the morning of 18 December and drive across the border into Kuwait, under the 2008 agreement that all American forces were to be out before the end of the year. What remains are the embassy's staff, just over a hundred military personnel and 4,000–5,000 private military contractors.

A war in the Democratic Republic of the Congo that drew in nine African countries and about 25 armed groups, and has therefore been called “Africa's world war”. Rwanda and Uganda supported rebels against President Laurent-Désiré Kabila, while Angola, Zimbabwe and Namibia, among others, defended his government. According to the most cited estimate, millions of people died, most of them from disease and malnutrition, but the figure is disputed.

title.en: About the end of the war

text.en: Wikipedia states that the war ended on 18 July 2003, when the transitional government took office. Wikidata gives 30 June 2003. The agreement that formally ended the war, the Global and All-Inclusive Agreement, was signed in December 2002; Wikipedia gives both 16 and 17 December in different places.

intro.en: Laurent-Désiré Kabila had taken power in May 1997, in the First Congo War, with the help of Rwanda, Uganda and groups in eastern Congo. Many Congolese soon saw him as a tool of foreign powers. In July 1998 Kabila dismissed his Rwandan army chief James Kabarebe for fear of a coup, and on 27 July he ordered the Rwandan troops to leave the country. The Banyamulenge, Congolese Tutsis in eastern Congo, felt threatened, and on 2 August soldiers in Goma rebelled with the support of Rwanda and Uganda. Rwanda claimed that Kabila was preparing a new genocide of Tutsis in Kivu. According to the source, it is still debated to what extent Rwanda wanted to protect the Banyamulenge and to what extent it had regional ambitions of its own. The trade in so-called conflict minerals influenced and financed the war.

members.en: The government of the Democratic Republic of the Congo under Laurent-Désiré Kabila and, from 2001, his son Joseph Kabila, with troops from Angola, Zimbabwe, Namibia and Chad (Sudan was also alleged to have taken part). Hutu militias such as the Interahamwe and the FDLR and local Mai-Mai militias also fought on the government's side.

Rwanda, Uganda and Burundi and the rebel groups they supported: the RCD (Rassemblement congolais pour la démocratie), which was dominated by the Banyamulenge and later split, and the MLC (Mouvement de libération du Congo) with support from Uganda. Rwanda and Uganda later also fought each other over the city of Kisangani.

outcome.en: The war ended without any military victor. The Lusaka Ceasefire Agreement of 1999 largely froze the front lines, but the fighting continued. After Laurent-Désiré Kabila was assassinated in January 2001, Joseph Kabila took over and negotiated. In 2002 came the Sun City Agreement on a joint government, the Pretoria Agreement with Rwanda and the Luanda Agreement with Uganda, and in October 2002 Rwanda announced that all of its roughly 20,000 soldiers had left Congo. On 18 July 2003 a transitional government took office in which the former warring parties were included, and in 2006 the first elections were held. Violence nevertheless continued in eastern Congo, in the conflicts in Ituri and Kivu. A UN expert panel accused Rwanda, Uganda and Zimbabwe in 2001 of systematically exploiting Congo's natural resources; Rwanda and Uganda rejected the accusations in the panel's 2002 report.

casualties.en: Estimates differ widely. The aid organisation International Rescue Committee (IRC) estimated in 2008 that the war and its consequences led to about 5.4 million more deaths than normal in 1998–2008, most through disease and malnutrition. The IRC also counted over 350,000 deaths from violence in 1998–2001. The Human Security Report Project at Simon Fraser University in Canada questioned the calculation and arrived at about 860,000 war-related deaths, while one of the IRC's authors has defended the study. The UCDP research programme at Uppsala University counts considerably fewer direct deaths in fighting: 7,336–12,106 battle-related deaths in the conflict between Congo's government and the rebels of the RCD and MLC in 1998–2001 (best estimate 8,018). In addition there is fighting in Congo that UCDP counts under other conflicts, for example Rwanda's government against the Hutu militia ALiR and Uganda's government against the ADF and LRA. UCDP counts only deaths in fighting between organised parties, including civilians killed in the fighting, but not deliberate violence against civilians or indirect deaths from disease and starvation. The difference shows that most of the deaths in the war did not occur in fighting. About 2 million people were driven from their homes.

summary.en: On 2 August 1998, Banyamulenge soldiers in Goma rise up against President Kabila, backed by Rwanda. The same month the rebel group RCD is formed with the support of Rwanda and Uganda, and it quickly takes control of large parts of eastern Congo, including the towns of Bukavu and Uvira. On 23 August Kisangani falls. In Kinshasa the government incites violence against Tutsis.

text.en: The uprising has no entry of its own in Wikidata, so the event could not be compared with a second source. Wikidata gives the same start date for the whole war, 2 August 1998.

caption.en: Illustration in the style of a documentary newspaper illustration from the 1970s, not a historical image.

summary.en: On 4 August 1998, Rwandan and Ugandan troops land in hijacked civilian aircraft in the middle of the Kitona air base on the Atlantic coast. Supported by defecting Congolese soldiers, they take the port city of Matadi and the power station at Inga, which supplies Kinshasa with electricity, and advance towards the capital. Zimbabwean and Angolan troops halt the attack, and the Rwandan forces withdraw to Angola and are later flown home.

On 5–10 June 2000, Ugandan and Rwandan troops, who had previously been allies, fight over the city of Kisangani. Large parts of the city are damaged. According to the human rights organisation Justice et Libération in Kisangani, around 1,000 people died, most of them civilians, and at least 3,000 were injured; another estimate in the source gives 1,576 dead. The fighting ended with a ceasefire negotiated by the UN.

On 16 January 2001, President Laurent-Désiré Kabila is shot in the Palais de Marbre in Kinshasa. According to the most common view, he was shot by one of his bodyguards, an 18-year-old former child soldier. The circumstances are unclear, and there are several unproven theories about foreign backers. His son Joseph Kabila becomes president and begins peace talks.

On 18 July 2003, the Congolese transitional government takes office, with the government and the former rebel groups included under the peace agreement of December 2002. The Congolese flag is raised in the rebel-held city of Goma, and the war is officially over. Violence nevertheless continues in eastern Congo.

text.en: The event has no entry with a date in Wikidata, so it could not be compared with a second source. Wikidata gives a different end date for the whole war, 30 June 2003.

summary.en: On 26 April 1986, reactor 4 at the Chernobyl Nuclear Power Plant near Pripyat in the Ukrainian SSR, then part of the Soviet Union, explodes. The accident causes a large release of radioactive material and is rated level 7, the highest level on the International Nuclear Event Scale. The area around the plant became an exclusion zone.

On 9 November 1989, the East German leadership announces at a live press conference, led by Günter Schabowski, that East Germans may travel freely. The announcement comes too early, and that same night the Berlin Wall, which East Germany began building on 13 August 1961, is opened. On 3 October 1990 Germany is reunified.

caption.en: Checkpoint Charlie in Berlin on the night the wall was opened, 10 November 1989. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 DE.

summary.en: On 11 February 1990, Nelson Mandela leaves Victor Verster Prison near Paarl, after a total of 27 years in prison. He was arrested in 1962 and sentenced to life imprisonment in the Rivonia Trial. President F. W. de Klerk has just legalised the banned parties and releases Mandela unconditionally. Mandela then drives through the crowds to the City Hall in Cape Town and gives a speech.

caption.en: Nelson Mandela and US President George H. W. Bush in the White House on 25 June 1990, four months after his release. Not from the release itself. License: Public domain.

summary.en: On 8 December 1991, the leaders of the Russian SFSR, the Byelorussian SSR and the Ukrainian SSR sign the Belovezha Accords on dissolving the Soviet Union. On 25 December Mikhail Gorbachev resigns, and that evening the Soviet flag is lowered over the Kremlin for the last time. The following day the Soviet of the Republics of the Supreme Soviet declares that the union has ceased to exist. The Soviet Union becomes 15 independent states.

caption.en: Leonid Kravchuk, Stanislav Shushkevich and Boris Yeltsin at the signing of the Belovezha Accords on 8 December 1991. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: On 6 April 1994, the plane carrying Rwanda's president Juvénal Habyarimana and Burundi's president Cyprien Ntaryamira is shot down as it is about to land in Kigali. Who fired is disputed. From 7 April, Hutu militias and extremists kill members of the Tutsi people, and also moderate Hutus and Twa. Between about 520,000 and 700,000 people are killed. The genocide ends in July 1994, when the rebel movement RPF defeats the government forces.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the genocide lasted until 19 July 1994 and Wikidata until 4 July 1994. Most researchers estimate the number of dead at 520,000–700,000. Rwanda's constitution gives over one million, and Wikidata gives one million.

caption.en: Remains and clothing of people killed in the church at Ntarama during the genocide. The site is now a memorial. Photo from 2006. License: CC BY 2.0.

summary.en: On 26–29 April 1994, the first election in South Africa in which citizens of all population groups may vote is held. The election concludes the four-year process that ended apartheid. The ANC wins 62.65 per cent of the votes, and the new National Assembly elects Nelson Mandela president, the first Black person to lead the country. He is inaugurated at the Union Buildings in Pretoria on 10 May 1994.

caption.en: Nelson Mandela votes in the election in April 1994, at Ohlange School in Inanda near Durban. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0.

summary.en: On 11 September 2001, 19 al-Qaeda terrorists hijack four passenger planes in the USA. Two are flown into the north and south towers of the World Trade Center in New York and one into the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia. The fourth crashes in a field near Shanksville in Pennsylvania after the passengers have revolted. 2,977 people are killed. The USA responds by invading Afghanistan and launching what is called the war on terror.

caption.en: Smoke rises from the towers of the World Trade Center in New York on 11 September 2001. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

summary.en: On 26 December 2004 at 07.58 local time, an earthquake of magnitude 9.1–9.3 occurs off the west coast of Aceh in northern Sumatra. The tsunami kills an estimated 227,898 people in 14 countries, particularly in Aceh in Indonesia, in Sri Lanka, in Tamil Nadu in India and in Khao Lak in Thailand.

caption.en: A destroyed village near the coast of Sumatra in Indonesia, photographed from the air on 2 January 2005, a week after the tsunami. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: The financial crisis begins in 2007 with a crisis in high-risk American mortgages, so-called subprime loans, when securities linked to housing lose value. It reaches its peak on 15 September 2008, when the investment bank Lehman Brothers in New York files for bankruptcy, the largest bankruptcy in US history. The crisis worsens the global downturn known as the Great Recession.

caption.en: The Lehman Brothers headquarters in New York on 15 September 2008, the day the bank filed for bankruptcy. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

summary.en: In December 2010, protests begin in the town of Sidi Bouzid in Tunisia, after Mohamed Bouazizi sets himself on fire. The protests spread across the Arab world. During 2011 the leaders of Tunisia, Egypt and Libya are overthrown, and in 2012 the president of Yemen. Civil wars follow in Syria, Libya and Yemen. The first wave ebbs out during 2012.

caption.en: Demonstrators face the police on Avenue Habib Bourguiba in Tunis on 20 January 2011. Licence: CC BY 2.0.

summary.en: On 12 December 2015, the countries of the world adopt the Paris Agreement by consensus at the COP21 climate conference in Le Bourget in Paris. The goal is to keep global warming well below 2 °C compared with pre-industrial times and to pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5 °C. The agreement enters into force on 4 November 2016 and has 194 parties.

caption.en: Heads of delegation at the UN climate conference COP21 in Paris on 30 November 2015, the first day of the conference. The agreement was adopted on 12 December. License: CC BY 2.0.

summary.en: In December 2019, an outbreak of a new disease begins in Wuhan in China. It is caused by the coronavirus SARS-CoV-2 and is named COVID-19. The WHO declares an international health emergency on 30 January 2020 and calls the outbreak a pandemic on 11 March 2020. The emergency is lifted on 5 May 2023. Over seven million deaths have been reported, and estimates of how many actually died range between 18.5 and 35.2 million.

text.en: Wikipedia states that the outbreak began in December 2019, whereas Wikidata states that the epidemic began on 17 November 2019.

caption.en: The SARS-CoV-2 virus in a scientific illustration from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, CDC, January 2020. Not a photograph. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 16 September 1987, the countries in Montréal agree to phase out CFCs and other substances that break down the ozone layer. The protocol enters into force in 1989 and becomes the first treaty in the history of the UN that every country has ratified, with 198 parties. The ozone hole over Antarctica is slowly healing, and the ozone layer is expected to be back at its 1980 level between 2040 and 2066.

caption.en: The ozone hole over Antarctica on 15 October 1987, measured by the satellite NOAA-9, the same autumn the Montreal Protocol was adopted. Licence: Public domain.

summary.en: On 1 January 1999, the euro was introduced as an account currency on the financial markets, for bank transfers and electronic payments. The exchange rates between the currencies of the first eleven participating countries were then fixed. Euro banknotes and coins did not arrive until 1 January 2002, and after about two months they had replaced the old national currencies. The euro is managed by the European Central Bank and the central banks of the euro area countries.

The Summer Olympics are held in Sydney from 15 September to 1 October 2000. It is the second time the Games are held in Australia and in the Southern Hemisphere; the first was in Melbourne in 1956. Teams from 199 countries take part, and these are the first Games with at least 300 events. The USA wins the medal table ahead of Russia and China, and the host nation Australia comes fourth.

On Saturday 7 February 2009, a series of forest and bush fires burn across the state of Victoria in extreme fire weather; up to 400 individual fires are recorded that day, which is called Black Saturday. 173 people die, the greatest loss of life in a bushfire in Australia's history. Over 2,000 homes are destroyed. The fires continue until mid-March, and a royal commission is appointed afterwards.

text.en: Wikipedia states 173 dead, whereas Wikidata states 231 dead.

summary.en: On 22 February 2011 at 12.51 local time, Christchurch is struck by an earthquake of magnitude 6.2, with its centre about 6.7 km south-east of the city centre. 185 people die, and the central city and the eastern suburbs are severely damaged, partly because buildings had already been weakened by an earthquake in September 2010. In the eastern suburbs, liquefaction causes great damage.

After Thursday 29 December 2011, Samoa goes straight to Saturday 31 December, so that Friday 30 December never occurs there. The country switches from UTC−11 to UTC+13 and ends up west of the date line instead of east of it. The prime minister said the change would make trade easier with New Zealand, Australia, China and other parts of Asia. Since then, Samoa has been one of the first places on Earth where each new day begins.

In the summer of 2016, the Great Barrier Reef, the world's largest coral reef system, suffers mass coral bleaching because of a marine heatwave. The northern part is hit hardest: large parts of a stretch about 800 km long die during the year because of the high water temperatures, and in the hardest-hit northern section about 67 per cent of the corals die. The researchers behind a study in Nature in 2017 link the event to climate change.

Between 23 November and 7 December 2019, a non-binding referendum is held in the autonomous region of Bougainville on greater self-government within Papua New Guinea or full independence. 98.31 per cent vote for independence. The vote is based on a 2001 agreement that ended the civil war of 1988–1998, but the final decision lies with the government of Papua New Guinea.

On 15 March 2019, during Friday prayers, two terrorist attacks with firearms take place in Christchurch, first at the Al Noor Mosque and shortly afterwards at the Linwood Islamic Centre. 51 people are killed, making it the deadliest attack in New Zealand's modern history. The attacks were directed at Muslims and immigrants and were driven mainly by white nationalism. The government bans semi-automatic weapons, and a new firearms law is passed in April 2019.

The underwater volcano Hunga Tonga–Hunga Haʻapai in Tonga erupts in December 2021 and reaches a very powerful climax on 15 January 2022. The explosion is the largest in the atmosphere ever measured with modern instruments, and the eruption is the largest since Pinatubo in 1991. The tsunami reaches Tonga, Fiji, Samoa, Vanuatu, New Zealand, Japan, the USA, Chile and Peru, among others, and people die in Tonga and in Peru.

Hurricane Katrina forms on 23 August 2005 near the Bahamas, reaches category 5 over the Gulf of Mexico and on 29 August makes landfall in Louisiana as a powerful category 3 hurricane. About 80 per cent of New Orleans is flooded, and most of the deaths result from the levees around the city failing because of design flaws. According to a revised count, 1,392 people die, and Katrina becomes the costliest tropical cyclone in US history.

text.en: Wikipedia states 1,392 dead after the US National Hurricane Center revised the figure in 2023; Wikidata gives the earlier estimate of 1,833 dead.

summary.en: On 12 January 2010 at 16.53 local time, Haiti is struck by an earthquake of magnitude 7.0, with its epicentre near Léogâne, about 25 km west of the capital Port-au-Prince. About three million people are affected. Estimates of the number of dead are disputed and range from 100,000–160,000 to the government's 220,000–316,000. The presidential palace, the parliament building and the cathedral in Port-au-Prince are severely damaged or destroyed.

On 9 July 2002, the African Union (AU) is launched in Durban in South Africa, with Thabo Mbeki of South Africa as its first chairperson. The union replaces the Organisation of African Unity (OAU), which was formed in 1963 and is dissolved the same day. The union had been proclaimed in the Sirte Declaration in Libya on 9 September 1999. Today it has 55 member states.

text.en: Wikidata gives 9 September 1999 as the founding of the union, the day of the Sirte Declaration. Wikipedia describes 1999 as the year the union was proclaimed and 9 July 2002 as the day it was launched.

summary.en: After the Second Liberian Civil War, Ellen Johnson Sirleaf stands in the presidential election of 2005. In the second round she receives 59 per cent of the votes against 40 per cent for the former footballer George Weah. On 23 November 2005 she is declared the winner and becomes the first woman elected president of an African country. She takes office on 16 January 2006 and receives the Nobel Peace Prize in 2011.

From 11 June to 11 July 2010, the men's football World Cup is played in South Africa, the first country in Africa to host the tournament. 32 teams play at ten stadiums in nine cities, and the opening match and the final are played at Soccer City in Johannesburg. Spain beat the Netherlands 1–0 after extra time in the final and win their first World Cup title.

In a referendum on 9–15 January 2011, which followed from a peace agreement, 98.83 per cent of those taking part vote for South Sudan to separate from Sudan. On 9 July 2011 South Sudan becomes independent, as Africa's 54th independent country. On 14 July the same year the country becomes the 193rd member of the UN. Some disputes with Sudan remain, including over oil revenues and the Abyei area.

The Ebola epidemic in West Africa is the most widespread outbreak of the disease in history. The first cases are recorded in Guinea in December 2013, and a small child who died in the village of Méliandou is widely regarded as the first case. The disease spreads mainly to Liberia and Sierra Leone, and the number of cases is at its highest in October 2014. Over 28,000 people are infected and over 11,000 die, and the WHO believes the true extent is larger. On 9 June 2016 the epidemic is declared over.

On 21 March 2018, 44 of the African Union's 55 member states sign the agreement on an African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) in Kigali in Rwanda. The agreement enters into force on 30 May 2019, and trading under the agreement officially begins on 1 January 2021. The countries promise to remove tariffs on most goods and services over 5 to 13 years. Measured by number of member countries, it is the world's largest free trade area after the WTO.

On 4 November 2008, the Democrat Barack Obama, senator from Illinois, wins the US presidential election together with Joe Biden. They defeat the Republicans John McCain and Sarah Palin. Obama becomes the first African American elected president. Shortly before midnight he gives his victory speech to about 250,000 people in Grant Park in Chicago.

On 5 August 2010, the San José mine in the Atacama Desert, about 45 kilometres north of Copiapó in Chile, collapses. 33 miners are trapped about 700 metres underground. Seventeen days after the accident a note comes up with a drill: the 33 are well in the shelter. On 13 October 2010, 69 days after the collapse, they are all hoisted up one at a time in a specially built capsule, while an estimated 5.3 million people follow it via live video.

After negotiations that formally began in September 2012 and were mostly held in Havana in Cuba, Colombia's president Juan Manuel Santos and the FARC leader Rodrigo Londoño (Timochenko) sign a peace agreement in Cartagena on 26 September 2016. In a referendum on 2 October, 50.2 per cent vote no to the agreement. A revised agreement is signed on 24 November and approved by Congress on 29 and 30 November, officially ending the conflict that began in 1964.

From 5 to 21 August 2016, the Summer Olympics are held in Rio de Janeiro, the first Olympic Games in South America and in a Portuguese-speaking country. Athletes from 207 nations compete for 306 sets of medals in 28 sports, and Kosovo, South Sudan and a refugee team take part for the first time. Maracanã is the main venue of the Games. The USA wins the most golds (46), and the host nation Brazil achieves its best Olympic result with seven golds.

On 30 July 1980, the New Hebrides became the independent republic of Vanuatu. Since 1887 the islands had been jointly ruled by Britain and France, with two separate administrations. Independence came in the midst of the brief “Coconut War”, in which Jimmy Stevens tried to break away the island of Espiritu Santo. The rebellion ended after troops from Papua New Guinea had been sent there.

On 10 July 1985, agents of the French intelligence service DGSE sank the Greenpeace ship Rainbow Warrior in Auckland harbour. The ship was to protest against a planned French nuclear test at Moruroa. The photographer Fernando Pereira drowned. France's defence minister Charles Hernu resigned, and France had to apologise and pay compensation.

On 3 June 1992, Australia's highest court, the High Court, decided the case that Eddie Mabo and others had brought against the state of Queensland. The court recognised for the first time Indigenous peoples' right to land, native title, and rejected the idea that Australia was terra nullius, nobody's land, when the British arrived. The following year a native title act was passed.

On 13 December 1986 Parliament unanimously passes the Constitution Act 1986, which applies from 1 January 1987. The act replaces the constitution of 1852 and the Westminster act of 1947, and it removes the British Parliament's ability to make laws for New Zealand. It sets out the roles of the monarch, the governor-general, ministers and judges. Even so, New Zealand has no written constitution in a single document, but a number of acts.

text.en: The day comes only from Wikipedia. Wikidata gives only the year, so only the year is shown here.

summary.en: With the Maori Language Act 1987 (Te Ture mō te Reo Māori), Māori, te reo Māori, becomes an official language of New Zealand, and its speakers gain the right to use it in legal settings such as courts. The act also establishes a language commission, which in 1991 was given the name Te Taura Whiri i te Reo Māori. It came after many years of Māori campaigning and partly in response to the Waitangi Tribunal's finding that the language is a treasure (taonga) protected by the treaty. The act was replaced in 2016 by a new language act.

text.en: Wikidata says that the act received royal assent on 20 July 1987. Wikipedia gives only the year, so only the year is shown here.

summary.en: In the first major settlement of historical claims to confiscated land (raupatu), Waikato-Tainui receive redress worth 170 million dollars, in cash and land owned by the Crown. The settlement act contains the Crown's formal apology for the invasion of the Waikato and for the indiscriminate confiscations that followed. Queen Elizabeth II gave it royal assent in person during her visit to New Zealand in 1995.

text.en: Wikipedia says that the settlement was agreed in 1995. The Danish encyclopaedia Lex writes that the Tainui agreement was signed in 1996.

summary.en: Greenland had joined the EC together with Denmark in 1973, even though a large majority of Greenlanders had voted no. In a referendum in 1982 a narrow majority voted to leave the Community, mainly because of fishing. The withdrawal took effect in 1985.

After a referendum in November 2008, in which about three out of four voted yes, the act on Greenland's self-government came into force on the national day, 21 June 2009. Greenlanders were recognised as a people with the right to independence, and Greenlandic became the sole official language.

text.en: The sources give different days for the referendum: Lex 5 November 2008 and Wikipedia 25 November 2008. Lex gives the share of yes votes as 75% in one article and about 76% in another.

summary.en: Malmöhus County and Kristianstad County, into which Scania had been divided since 1719, are merged into Skåne County. The county seat is Malmö.
The fixed link across the Øresund between Amager and Scania is inaugurated. It consists of a tunnel, an artificial island and a bridge, and carries a motorway and a double-track railway.
On 26 August 1993 the Sámi Parliament of Sweden is established, with its seat in Kiruna. It is both an elected body for the Sámi and a government agency.
On 1 January 1995 Sweden becomes a member of the European Union, together with Finland and Austria. In the referendum of 13 November 1994, 52.7 per cent of valid votes were yes.

On 2 July 1997 the government of Thailand was forced to float the baht, because the country no longer had enough foreign currency to hold its peg to the US dollar. Capital fled almost at once, and the crisis spread across much of East and Southeast Asia. South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand were hit hardest, and Hong Kong, Laos, Malaysia and the Philippines were also hurt. Currencies and stock markets fell and private debt rose steeply. The recovery in 1998–1999 was nevertheless rapid.

In March 2001 the Taliban destroyed the two giant Buddha statues carved into the cliff in the Bamiyan Valley. The Taliban leader Mullah Muhammad Omar had ordered on 26 February that all statues in Afghanistan be destroyed. According to radiocarbon dating, the smaller statue was built between 544 and 595 and the larger between 591 and 644. The destruction was condemned in Afghanistan and around the world. In 2003 the site became a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

On 12–13 March 2013 the cardinals gathered in the Sistine Chapel to elect a successor to Benedict XVI, who had resigned on 28 February. Of 117 eligible cardinal electors, all but two took part. On the fifth ballot they elected Jorge Mario Bergoglio, archbishop of Buenos Aires, who took the name Francis. He was the first Jesuit and the first Latin American pope, and the first pope born or raised outside Europe since Gregory III in the 8th century.

In 1983–1985 Ethiopia was struck by a severe famine. In the autumn of 1984 Tigray, Wollo and Eritrea were hit hardest, and Begemder was affected too. The causes were drought, the civil war and the policies of the military regime, the Derg, which according to the source deliberately made the famine worse; Human Rights Watch holds that more than half of the deaths were due to human rights abuses. In 1985 and 1986 about 600,000 people were moved, many by force, and according to Human Rights Watch at least 50,000 died as a result of the forced resettlement. Estimates of how many died in the famine range from about 300,000 to 1.2 million. A BBC report in October 1984 and the Live Aid concert in July 1985 made the famine known around the world and raised aid.

In 1988 the World Meteorological Organization (WMO) and the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) set up the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, IPCC, and the UN endorsed it the same year. The panel's secretariat is in Geneva. The IPCC assesses research on climate change for the world's governments. In 2007 the IPCC shared the Nobel Peace Prize with Al Gore.

On 4 June 1992 the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change was opened for signature at the UN Conference on Environment and Development in Rio de Janeiro on 3–14 June, known as the Earth Summit. By 12 June 154 countries had signed. The convention's objective is to stabilise the concentration of greenhouse gases in the air at a level that prevents dangerous human interference with the climate. The convention entered into force in 1994.

On 11 December 1997 the Kyoto Protocol was adopted in Kyoto, Japan. It built on the 1992 climate convention and committed the developed countries that joined to reduce their emissions of greenhouse gases, among them carbon dioxide and methane. The protocol entered into force on 16 February 2005. The United States never ratified it, and Canada withdrew in 2012.

On 13 December 2006 the leaders of a six-week expedition on the Yangtze River declared the river dolphin baiji functionally extinct. No dolphins had been found, and if any remained there were too few for the species to survive. The population fell sharply as China industrialised and made ever heavier use of the river for fishing, shipping and hydroelectric power. The IUCN lists the baiji as critically endangered and possibly extinct.

After the death of the reform-minded former party leader Hu Yaobang in April 1989, students and workers gathered in Tiananmen Square in Beijing. They demanded, among other things, action against corruption and inflation, and the students called for democracy and freedom of the press and of speech. On 17 May about one million people were in the square, and the protests spread to some 400 cities. The government declared martial law on 20 May. During the night of 3 to 4 June the army moved into central Beijing, and many demonstrators, bystanders and soldiers were killed, most of them along Chang’an Avenue west of the square. Estimates of the number of dead range from several hundred to a few thousand. Many were then arrested, and the events are today among the most censored topics in China.

text.en: The government’s figure shortly afterwards was about 300 dead, and on 19 June 241 confirmed deaths were reported. Records from Beijing’s eleven main hospitals showed at least 478 dead, Amnesty International estimated from several hundred to close to 1,000, and the Swiss ambassador estimated 2,700. The group Tiananmen Mothers has identified 202 dead. Wikidata gives both 300 and 400 dead. The government says that no one died in the square itself; according to the source most deaths occurred outside the square.
